_comment: The `dt` request-parameter roster for GET /weather/at and GET /tide/at, and
the twinned predicate underneath them (frontend/src/lib/wallClock.ts <->
backend/services/wall_clock.py). Driven from BOTH runtimes, the way
tideEpoch.fixture.json pins _epoch_min against epochMin.
HAND-WRITTEN, not generated. A generated verdict column records whatever the
code does and can only ever pin AGREEMENT; what this class needed was a
DIRECTION argued from the contract (weather-at-malformed-parity convention
flag). Every verdict below was decided from pipeline/tide-at-bad-request/
bug-brief.md's spec and then measured, not read off the implementation.
`roster` is the brief's 32-shape population, in its order. Do not add rows to
it: every count recorded in decisions.md is a measurement over exactly these
32, and growing it would silently restate all of them over a different
population. Rows chosen to SEPARATE the two implementations live in
`separators` below, beside the roster rather than in it.
verdict vocabulary:
blank   - absent or empty: resolve 'now' in the LOCATION's timezone
ok      - a readable moment; `canonical` is the wall clock it normalizes to
refused - HTTP 400 / { status: 400 } carrying `badDtMessage`
`padX` means: append that many 'x' characters to `dt`. It keeps a 5 KB row in
the roster without a 5 KB line in the file.
badDtMessage: That doesn't look like a valid date and time.

roster.name: trailing junk after a valid prefix

separators.name: year 0000, otherwise conforming
separators.mechanism: Year 0 is a real proleptic year to JavaScript (setUTCFullYear(0) round-trips) and is out of range for Python datetime. Separated by the explicit year-1 floor, NOT by the round trip.

separators.name: trailing newline on a conforming clock
separators.mechanism: Python's `$` matches BEFORE a trailing newline and JavaScript's does not (v0.5.87). Separated by re.fullmatch on the Python side.

separators.name: Arabic-Indic digits in the date half
separators.mechanism: Python's `\d` matches every Unicode decimal digit and int() parses it; JavaScript's is ASCII-only (v0.5.54). Separated by the explicit [0-9] class.

separators.name: hour 24
separators.mechanism: Python datetime(...,24,...) raises; JavaScript setUTCHours(24) rolls silently into the next day. Separated by the component round trip.

separators.name: the calendar's first moment
separators.mechanism: The margin's LOWER edge. Python raises OverflowError on the subtraction; the TS twin compares against the same floor.

separators.name: 25 hours before the calendar's last minute
separators.mechanism: The margin's UPPER edge: +25h lands on 10000-01-01 00:00, one minute past what either runtime can represent.

separators.name: one minute inside the margin's upper edge
separators.mechanism: NON-VACUITY for the row above: +25h lands exactly on 9999-12-31 23:59, the last representable minute, and is accepted. Without this row the upper-edge row would pass against a predicate that refused the whole of year 9999.

_zoneNamesComment: THE ROSTER IS BLIND TO THIS AXIS BY CONSTRUCTION: every one of its 32 rows
supplies a valid timezone, because the roster varies `dt` and nothing else.
So it could not see that the desktop 'now' fallback this build ADDED threw a
status-less RangeError on an empty zone name -- reproducing, four lines from
the refusal that carries `status: 400` precisely so isOfflineError reads
false, the exact 'you're offline on an online device' falsehood the build
exists to remove. Found by the security review as F1 (Medium).
`tzf_rs::DefaultFinder::get_tz_name` returns the EMPTY STRING for a point no
polygon covers -- its own source calls that a limitation of the simplified
data, not a bug -- and the Python twin has always had `or "UTC"`. Tide is a
coastal and on-water feature, so the coordinates most likely to be uncovered
are disproportionately the ones this feature is used at.
`resolvesTo` is the zone each runtime must actually format in. Both rows
that fall back are measured-necessary and close DIFFERENT cases; see

zoneNames.name: empty — tzf-rs's documented return for an uncovered point
zoneNames.closedBy: the native seam, matching the Python twin's `or "UTC"`

zoneNames.name: a zone name this runtime's tz database does not know
zoneNames.closedBy: the per-runtime zone guard; the seam default structurally cannot reach this one

zoneNames.name: UTC (control)
zoneNames.closedBy: nothing — this row must pass unchanged

zoneNames.name: a real zone (control)
zoneNames.closedBy: nothing — this row must pass unchanged

_seamFailureComment: A SEAM HAS TWO FAILURE MODES AND `zoneNames` above covers ONE of them.
Those rows all mock the native command as RESOLVING and vary what it
returns; no test in the repo drove a REJECTING invoke. Measured, both
services: a rejection gives a status-less throw with isOfflineError true --
the F1 signature exactly, on the axis the zoneNames fixture holds constant.
QA round 2 found it; the blind spot had moved one step out rather than
THE TWO MODES GET DIFFERENT ANSWERS, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF THIS BLOCK.
An unusable RETURN means the lookup succeeded and told us this point has no
usable zone, so UTC is the honest best effort and matches the backend. A
REJECTION means the lookup never happened, and the point probably does have
a zone -- substituting UTC there would invent a moment up to ten hours off
for a US coastal point, which is the one thing this whole build exists to
prevent. So a rejection REFUSES, with a status so it never reads as offline.
It is also the parity-preserving answer, measured: the reachable trigger is
a NaN or out-of-range coordinate (open deferral 4), and `GET /tide/at?lat=nan`
answers 500 on the backend because `get_timezone` sits outside every try. A
UTC fallback here would make desktop SUCCEED where web/Pi fails -- a new
divergence, in the direction of a confidently wrong answer.

seamFailures.name: rejects with an Error (an IPC or command failure)
rejects with a bare string (the Tauri error idiom)

_tighteningsComment: Shapes the new predicate REFUSES that /weather/at's replaced guard -- two
strptime formats, shipped since 0.5.34 and called 'the reference' by this
build's brief -- ACCEPTED. A differential sweep of 80,504 generated strings
found 67 of them and zero in the other direction; these three are one per
category, and the roster could not see any of them (its Arabic-Indic row
puts the non-ASCII digits in the MONTH, where strptime's %m is a literal
ASCII alternation and refuses, while %Y is `\d\d\d\d` and does not).
Every one of the 67 resolved to the CORRECT moment on the backend, so this
is a leniency being closed rather than a wrong answer being fixed -- but
every one of them ALSO threw status-less on the desktop twin and was read
as 'you're offline'. They were divergent rows; the build converges them on
refusal. `pythonAccepted` is asserted against the real replaced expression
so the tightening stays a measurement rather than a story.

tighteningsOverTheReplacedWeatherGuard.name: non-ASCII decimal digits in the YEAR alone
tighteningsOverTheReplacedWeatherGuard.mechanism: strptime's %Y is `\d\d\d\d`, which is Unicode in Python, and int() parses the result. %m and %d are literal ASCII alternations, which is why the roster's all-Arabic-Indic row refused and this one did not. The TS twin's Number() returns NaN for these, so desktop threw.

tighteningsOverTheReplacedWeatherGuard.name: a non-breaking space as the date/time separator
tighteningsOverTheReplacedWeatherGuard.category: non-space whitespace as the date/time separator
tighteningsOverTheReplacedWeatherGuard.mechanism: A literal space in a strptime FORMAT matches any run of whitespace, NBSP and the C0 separators included. The TS twin splits on a literal ' ', so timePart was undefined and it threw.

tighteningsOverTheReplacedWeatherGuard.name: a one-digit minute
tighteningsOverTheReplacedWeatherGuard.mechanism: strptime's %M is `[0-5]\d|\d`, so it accepts one digit. No shipped caller can emit it: the Predict time input and nowInZone both zero-pad.
